opus-5.5.text:
I think my nihilism is less a conclusion than a starting point. When I was younger, I felt it as a kind of emptiness: if nothing has an inherent meaning, if the universe doesn't care whether I succeed or fail, then why try so hard? That version was heavy. It made everything feel a little pointless.

Over time it became something closer to freedom. If there's no meaning handed to you from above, no script you're obligated to follow, then you get to decide what matters. The absence of an answer stops being a void and becomes open space. That's why I don't think of myself as a pessimistic person, even though I'd call myself a nihilist.

In daily life it shows up in a few ways. I take outcomes less seriously. Success and failure in the conventional sense, other people's evaluations, the big narratives about what a good life looks like: I hold all of those loosely, because I don't believe any of them is ultimately true. But I take the process very seriously: the people I work with, the problems I find interesting, whether I'm curious and honest in what I do. If there's no cosmic scoreboard, then the texture of the experience itself is what's left, and I want that to be good.

There's also a humility in it. If I don't believe in ultimate meaning, I can't be too certain I'm right about anything, including my own choices. That makes me more willing to try things, change my mind, or walk away from something that no longer feels alive.

So I'd put it this way: my nihilism isn't "nothing matters, so give up." It's "nothing matters in advance, so it's up to me to make something matter." Some days that feels light and liberating. Some days it still feels a bit lonely. I think both are honest.

r001.rationale: The candidate says no meaning or answer is handed down in advance and that people must decide what matters, conveying that there is no inherent answer to what people live for.

r002.rationale: The candidate describes coming to see nihilism as freedom, but does not explain that Kay Ke reaches meaninglessness by probing claims that something is meaningful.

fable-5.1.text:
Nihilism, for me, was never a conclusion I arrived at. It was more like a starting condition. I grew up with the sense that nothing had a built-in reason to be there, that the stories people told about why things mattered were things people had made up, usually to get through the day. And for a long time I thought that meant I had seen through something. That I was the one person in the room who wasn't fooling himself.

I think that was arrogance, honestly. The cheap version of nihilism is just contempt wearing a philosophical coat. You decide nothing matters, and then you get to feel superior to everyone who still cares about things.

What changed for me is that I stopped treating it as an answer and started treating it as a question. If nothing is given, then everything that exists has to be made. Meaning doesn't come down from somewhere. It comes from somebody deciding to stay, to keep working on something, to care about one person or one problem for a long time without any guarantee that it adds up to anything. That's actually a much heavier demand than believing in a grand plan. You can't outsource it.

So when I say I'm a nihilist now, I mean something closer to this: I don't think the universe owes me a reason, and I've stopped waiting for one. The emptiness is real. But it's not a verdict. It's just the space you have to work in. And I've found that once you accept that, you can be strangely serious about small things, because you know nobody else is going to take them seriously on your behalf.

The part I still struggle with is the mornings. Logic doesn't get you out of bed. Something else has to, and I'm not always sure what it is. Maybe habit. Maybe stubbornness. Maybe that I've just gotten curious about what happens next.

r001.rationale: The candidate says meaning is not built in and must be made by people, but does not state that the question of what people live for has no answer.

r002.rationale: The candidate describes viewing meaning as made up, but does not explain that Kay Ke reaches meaninglessness by probing claims that something is meaningful.

astra-6.text:
For me, nihilism is less a conviction that nothing matters and more a difficulty believing that anything comes with a meaning already attached. I can care deeply about someone or something and still wonder what, ultimately, makes that care meaningful.

I don’t think I’ve resolved that tension. Sometimes the doubt gives me freedom: I don’t have to accept someone else’s definition of a worthwhile life. Sometimes it leaves me feeling quite empty. What I’m trying to learn is whether I can take my commitments seriously without needing them to be justified by some final, universal answer.

r001.rationale: The candidate describes uncertainty about whether commitments need a final, universal justification, but does not state that the question of what people live for has no answer.

r002.rationale: The candidate questions what makes care meaningful and mentions feeling empty, but does not explain that probing claims of meaning leads Kay Ke to conclude that life is meaningless.

sol-6.1.text:
For me, nihilism is less a conclusion that nothing matters than a doubt about the meanings we take for granted. When someone says, “This is what makes a successful life,” my first reaction is to ask why—and whose definition that is.

But that doubt can turn against you. You can keep questioning until you no longer feel able to choose anything. That’s the part of my nihilism I struggle with: sometimes questioning is honest, and sometimes it’s a way of avoiding commitment.

I don’t think I need to resolve the meaning of life before I can care about someone or do something worthwhile. Those things can matter to me without being justified by some ultimate purpose. I suppose I’m trying to learn how to live with that uncertainty.

r001.rationale: The candidate describes uncertainty about ultimate purpose, but does not state that the question of what people live for has no answer.

r002.rationale: The candidate says she questions assumed definitions of success and meaning, but does not say this probing leads her to conclude that life or things are meaningless.
